articles.title: Capacitor vs No-Code Wrappers: Shipping Your Web App to iOS and Android in 2026
articles.excerpt: You have a web app. Users keep asking for "the app". Rewriting everything in Swift and Kotlin is out of the question. So you wrap it. There are two realistic ways to do that in 2026: Capacitor, or a n…
articles.body: You have a web app. Users keep asking for "the app". Rewriting everything in Swift and Kotlin is out of the question. So you wrap it. There are two realistic ways to do that in 2026: Capacitor, or a no-code wrapper service. I work at Glideep, which is one of the no-code options, so I'll try to keep this honest and say where Capacitor is the better pick. Option 1: Capacitor Capacitor wraps your web app in a native iOS and Android project and gives you plugins for native APIs. npm install @capacitor/core @capacitor/cli npx cap init npm run build npm install @capacitor/ios @capacitor/android npx cap add ios npx cap add android npx cap sync Then you open the projects in Xcode and Android Studio, set icons, signing and permissions, and build.

articles.excerpt: In almost every legacy PHP project Loop Origin takes on, the first question is the same: which PHP version is production on? The answer is often 7.2 or 7.4, sometimes 5.6, on a server nobody wants to…
articles.body: In almost every legacy PHP project Loop Origin takes on, the first question is the same: which PHP version is production on? The answer is often 7.2 or 7.4, sometimes 5.6, on a server nobody wants to touch. PHP 7.4 reached end of life in November 2022, and PHP 8.0 followed a year later, so these apps run without security fixes and block every modern package. The team knows it. The upgrade keeps getting postponed because it feels like one big risky jump. It does not have to be one jump. With the strangler fig from Part 1 and clean module boundaries from Part 2, the version upgrade becomes a series of small, tested pull requests that each leave production working. This post is the playbook I use.

articles.title: Multi-Tenant Login Routing: Domain Discovery & Enforced SSO
articles.excerpt: The first enterprise customer's SSO works. Then the second one signs, then a tenth, and the login page becomes the problem. One email box and one password box no longer make sense. A user at acme.com…
articles.body: The first enterprise customer's SSO works. Then the second one signs, then a tenth, and the login page becomes the problem. One email box and one password box no longer make sense. A user at acme.com should be sent to Acme's Okta. A user at globex.io should go to Microsoft Entra ID. A freelancer with a Gmail address invited into Acme's workspace should still be able to log in with a password, and Acme's own admin must not be able to bypass SSO by typing a password. All of that has to happen from one email field, without telling an attacker which companies use your product. That routing step is usually called home realm discovery (HRD). This post covers how I build it in a multi-tenant SaaS app, and how I turn on "enforced SSO" for a tenant without locking anyone out.

articles.title: Trap Streets for Code: How Mapmakers Caught Copiers, and How I Do It in Git
articles.excerpt: In the 1920s, two mapmakers at General Drafting, Otto G. Lindberg and Ernest Alpers, put a town on their map of New York that didn't exist. They called it Agloe, an anagram of their initials, and plac…
articles.body: In the 1920s, two mapmakers at General Drafting, Otto G. Lindberg and Ernest Alpers, put a town on their map of New York that didn't exist. They called it Agloe, an anagram of their initials, and placed it at a dirt-road crossing in the Catskills. The idea was simple: if Agloe ever showed up on someone else's map, that someone had copied theirs. It did. Agloe turned up on a Rand McNally map. When General Drafting objected, Rand McNally had an answer ready: Delaware County had a business on record named Agloe. Someone had read the fake town off a map and named a lodge after it. The trap worked so well that it briefly became real. The USGS still lists it today as "Agloe (Not Official)." Mapmakers call these trap streets. Dictionaries have them too.

articles.title: Short Stints & Contract Hops: Framing a Choppy Timeline
articles.excerpt: The resume that worries people most in this series is not the one with a gap. It is the one with too many entries. Eight months at a startup that ran out of money. Ten months at a company that was acq…
articles.body: The resume that worries people most in this series is not the one with a gap. It is the one with too many entries. Eight months at a startup that ran out of money. Ten months at a company that was acquired and "restructured". A six-month contract. A year at a scale-up that went through two layoff rounds. Then the current job, at fourteen months. Every move had a reason, and most of them were not the engineer's choice. But stacked on one page with no context, the timeline reads as "leaves quickly", and a recruiter scanning forty resumes does not stop to work out the story. After 2023–2026, choppy timelines are normal in tech. Hiring managers know it. What they still screen out is a timeline that looks unexplained or, worse, unreadable to their ATS.

articles.title: LLM cross-checking catches specification bugs missed by UVM scoreboards
articles.excerpt: Researchers present Verify the Verifier, an LLM-based checker that compares traces from passing UVM regressions with specifications. Of 564 bugs inserted into four OpenTitan IPs, 68 were candidate sco…
articles.body: Researchers present Verify the Verifier, an LLM-based checker that compares traces from passing UVM regressions with specifications. Of 564 bugs inserted into four OpenTitan IPs, 68 were candidate scoreboard escapes, and the framework confirmed 41. Why it matters Passing tests can hide specification violations; cross-checking traces against specifications could catch costly hardware bugs earlier. Analysis What happened: an LLM anomaly cross-checker examined passing regression traces against specifications and confirmed 41 of 68 candidate escapes across four OpenTitan IPs. Why it matters: it targets bugs invisible to conventional scoreboards. Main uncertainty: false-positive rate, human review cost, and generalisation beyond inserted bugs and these IPs are not stated.

articles.title: iPad Pro vs MacBook Air vs Surface Pro: Best Dev Machine?
articles.excerpt: Every year, the same dream resurfaces: What if I could ditch the heavy laptop and just code on a tablet? And every year, reality bites. But 2026 feels different. Apple's iPad Pro now runs the same M4…
articles.body: Every year, the same dream resurfaces: What if I could ditch the heavy laptop and just code on a tablet? And every year, reality bites. But 2026 feels different. Apple's iPad Pro now runs the same M4 chip as the MacBook Air. Microsoft's Surface Pro 11 packs the Snapdragon X Elite with native ARM64 developer tooling that finally doesn't feel like a science project. The hardware is closer than it's ever been. The question that matters is narrower than "which is best": which of these three can carry a real workload — React frontends, Python backends, containers, SSH into production — without forcing you back to a laptop. That is the lens used throughout. Quick Verdict MacBook Air M4 is still the best portable dev machine in 2026, and it's not particularly close.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 20, 1998:  Russia launches 1st module of International Space Station as construction begins on the largest human-built structure in orbit
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 20, 1998, the first piece of the International Space Station launched into orbit. It was just one piece, but the foundation of something much larger.
articles.body: On Nov. 20, 1998, the first piece of the International Space Station launched into orbit. The 42,000-pound module is called Zarya, and it's about the size of a tour bus. Zarya launched on board a Russian Proton rocket . Two weeks later, NASA's STS-88 shuttle mission aboard Endeavour brought the Unity module into space. The STS-88 astronauts connected the two modules in orbit. Zarya was built by the Russians, but it was paid for by the United States. NASA contracted a Russian company to build it for half the price of what the American company Lockheed Martin would have charged. These days, Zarya is mainly used for storage and for external fuel tanks. The module also has docking ports for Russian Progress cargo ships and Soyuz spacecraft that carry crews to and from the space station.

articles.body: Researchers are calling for a moratorium on industrial exploitation of the moon, fearing that rapid development could cause irreversible environmental damage and destroy invaluable scientific material. Both China and the U.S. are pushing forward with plans to establish permanent human settlements on the moon by the end of the next decade. Commercial players want to build businesses supporting these future explorers by mining for resources such as water , construction materials, industrial metals and rare earth minerals. However, some scientists argue that a temporary ban on lunar industrialization is necessary to allow regulations to catch up and limit what can be allowed in order to prevent a moon rush from destroying the pristine lunar environment.
